intuition: Build a factorization in increasing order. Try a divisor of the amount still left, pair it with the remaining quotient, and then try splitting that quotient further. Starting later choices at the current divisor avoids repeating the same factors in different orders.

At any remaining product r, a nontrivial factorization has a smallest factor no greater than sqrt(r). Search candidate divisors only up to that boundary. When factor divides remaining, the pair factor and remaining/factor already completes one valid answer after the current path. The quotient may itself split into more factors, so recurse to discover those longer answers.

The next recursive search starts at the selected factor, not at two. This permits repeated factors while preserving nondecreasing order. Emitting the pair before recursion covers the decomposition that leaves the quotient whole; recursion covers its further decomposition. A prime offers no divisor and produces no answer, while n=1 likewise has no permitted factorization.
The original n alone never appears because every emission introduces a divisor and a quotient.

steps: For n=12, search starts with remaining=12, minimum factor 2, and an empty path.
Factor 2 divides 12, yielding quotient 6. Emit [2,6] as a complete two-factor answer.
Recurse with path=[2] and remaining=6. Factor 2 divides it, so emit [2,2,3].
Return to the original search, undo the chosen 2, and try factor 3. It divides 12, emitting [3,4].
No further factor up to sqrt(12) remains. Return the three combinations, with their outer ordering irrelevant.

concept.question: How do increasing factors avoid reordered copies of the same product?
intuition: Trying factors in arbitrary order repeats collections such as 2×6 and 6×2. A number also may be broken into more than two factors.

Try a divisor no smaller than the previous factor. Pair it with the remaining quotient for one answer, then explore splitting that quotient further. Only divisors through its square root need to be tried; the larger counterpart is already the quotient.
concept.observation: Use factors greater than one in nondecreasing order, and split the remaining quotient further when possible.
approach: Try increasing divisors of the remaining product.
Save the chosen prefix plus a divisor and its quotient.
Continue splitting the quotient with no smaller future factors.
concept.correctness: Every nontrivial factor collection can be sorted into nondecreasing order. Its next smallest factor divides the remaining product and is no greater than the square root when at least two factors remain. The search tries that factor and can continue along the collection. Saving quotients covers final pairs, while increasing-order constraints prevent reordered duplicates.
